intro: Six under sink water filters ranked by the thing that matters most: what each one is independently certified to remove, not what the box says it removes.

Buy the Aquasana Claryum 3-Stage if you want one answer. It carries NSF/ANSI 42, 53 and 401 certification from the WQA, which covers lead, PFOA/PFOS and a long list of other health contaminants, and it fits under any standard kitchen sink in about an hour. Everything below explains when one of the other five is the better buy.
quickAnswer: An under sink water filter is the best balance of cost, capacity and filtration for drinking and cooking water. A pitcher holds a few cups and needs refilling all day; a whole-house system treats the water you flush and wash the car with, which you do not need to drink. An under sink system sits in the cabinet, treats only the water that comes out of one faucet, and does it at a cost per gallon that is far lower than a pitcher.

sections.h: The 6 Best Under Sink Water Filters in 2026 at a Glance

blocks.p: The problem is that the category is crowded with near-identical listings that make the same claims: 99% of lead, PFAS, heavy metals, microplastics. Those claims are often not backed by any certification at all. The quickest way through the noise is to ignore the box and look for the NSF/ANSI standard numbers, and the name of the body that tested the product. That is how this list is ranked.

If you want one answer, buy the **Aquasana Claryum 3-Stage**. It is certified to NSF/ANSI 42, 53 and 401, which covers chlorine taste, lead, PFOA/PFOS and a long list of other contaminants. If you want the same certification for less money, buy the **A.O. Smith AO-US-200**. If your water is already safe and simply tastes of chlorine, the **Waterdrop 10UA** is cheap to buy and cheap to run. If your water report shows high dissolved solids, nitrates or arsenic, carbon will not help and you need reverse osmosis: the **iSpring RCC7AK** with a tank, or the **Waterdrop G3P800** without one.

Before you buy any of them, find your utility's annual water quality report, often called a Consumer Confidence Report, or test a well. The report tells you whether you are solving a taste problem or a health problem, and that one fact decides most of this page. If you are still deciding between an under sink unit and treating the whole house, start with our [guide to the best water filtration systems for home](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/), which compares every type side by side.
THE RULE
Read the certification, not the claim.
A listing can say anything. An NSF/ANSI certification from NSF, WQA or IAPMO names the exact contaminants a filter was tested against. If a claim is not on the certification, treat it as unproven.

Drinking water filters in North America are certified against a short list of standards written by NSF International and the American National Standards Institute. The certification itself is done by an accredited body, usually NSF, the Water Quality Association (WQA) or IAPMO R&T. All three are legitimate. What matters is which standard the product was tested to, and which contaminants are listed under it, because a filter can be certified to Standard 53 for lead but not for PFAS, or the other way around.

Standard 42 covers aesthetic effects: chlorine taste and odor, chloramine, and particulates. It is the most common certification on cheap filters, and it is a perfectly good one if taste is your only complaint. It says nothing about health contaminants. The Waterdrop 10UA, for example, holds Standard 42 for chlorine taste and odor, which is exactly what it is good at.

Standard 53 is the one that matters for lead, cysts, volatile organic compounds and, under protocol P473, PFOA and PFOS. A filter certified to Standard 53 has been tested against a defined challenge level of each listed contaminant over its full rated capacity. When a product says it is certified to 53, look at which contaminants are listed. Both of our top two picks carry 53 with lead and P473.

Standard 401 covers so-called incidental or emerging compounds: certain pharmaceuticals, herbicides, flame retardants and BPA at the trace levels found in some tap water. It is a useful extra rather than a must-have, but it is a reliable sign that a maker paid for broad testing.

Standard 58 is the reverse osmosis standard, centred on total dissolved solids, and it can also list arsenic, nitrate, fluoride and other reductions. Standard 372 is often misread: it certifies that the materials in contact with water are lead-free. It does not say the filter removes lead from the water. When a listing leans on 372 and does not mention 53, it is not a lead-reduction claim.

sections.h: Under Sink Water Filters Compared Side by Side

blocks.p: The table lines up the six picks on the specs that decide which one fits your kitchen. Certification and flow figures are the makers' and certifiers' numbers, and filter life is the rated interval, which will be shorter if your water carries a lot of sediment or chlorine.

Three patterns stand out. First, certification and flow pull in opposite directions in carbon filters. The two systems with the broadest health certification are rated at 0.5 gpm, while the fastest carbon filter on the list does not show its certification on the maker's own page. That is not a coincidence: water that moves slowly through a carbon block spends longer in contact with it, which is what makes the deeper reductions possible.

Second, the cost of ownership is set by the filter life column, not the price of the system. A filter rated for 500 gallons that you replace twice a year costs more over three years than one rated for 12 months, even if the starter kit is cheaper. We look at that in more detail in the running-cost section below.

Third, the two RO systems are a different category. They reduce the dissolved minerals and salts that carbon cannot touch, and they cost more, use more space and send some water to the drain. Only choose RO if your water report gives you a reason to, and if you do, the tank-or-tankless decision is mostly about cabinet space and whether there is an outlet under the sink.

This is the single biggest decision in the category, and most people overbuy. Activated carbon works by adsorption: contaminants stick to the enormous internal surface of the carbon as water passes through. It is excellent at chlorine, chloramine, many organic chemicals, and, in a well-designed block, lead and PFAS. It does nothing for dissolved salts, nitrates, fluoride or hardness, because those are dissolved ions that do not bind to carbon.

Reverse osmosis forces water through a membrane with pores small enough to hold back most dissolved ions. That is why an RO system's certification is built around total dissolved solids, and why it can list arsenic, nitrate and fluoride reductions that no carbon filter can match. Every RO system on the market also includes carbon stages before and after the membrane, so you get the carbon benefits too.

The costs of RO are real, though. It sends water to the drain while it produces filtered water; modern tankless designs such as the Waterdrop G3P800 are rated at a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio, and older tank designs typically waste more. It takes more cabinet space, more installation time and, for tankless units, an electrical outlet. It also strips out calcium and magnesium, which is why many systems, including the iSpring RCC7AK, add a remineralization stage for taste.

The practical rule: on municipal water with a clean report, a certified carbon filter does everything you need. On a private well, or where the report shows nitrates, arsenic, high TDS or fluoride you want reduced, choose RO, and our [best reverse osmosis system guide](/best-reverse-osmosis-system/) compares tank, tankless and countertop units in depth. If you are unsure, test first. A lab test costs less than the difference between the two systems, and it stops you buying the wrong one.

One more distinction is worth knowing. Neither type softens water for the rest of the house. Hard water that scales your kettle will still scale your dishwasher and shower, because an under sink filter only treats one faucet. If scale on fixtures is the problem, a softener belongs on the main line, which our [home filtration guide](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/) covers in its whole-house section.

sections.h: Buying Guide: The Specs That Matter

blocks.p: Once you know whether you need carbon or RO, five specs separate a good under sink water filter system from a frustrating one. Read them in this order.

Find the standard numbers and the certifier. Then look at the contaminant list on the performance data sheet, which every certified filter is required to publish. If the contaminant you care about is not on it, the filter is not certified for it, whatever the listing says.

Certified reductions only hold up to the rated capacity. A family of four that drinks and cooks with filtered water typically uses somewhere between one and three gallons a day, which is roughly 365 to 1,100 gallons a year. Divide the filter's rated capacity by your daily use to get a realistic change interval, and use whichever comes first, the gallon limit or the time limit.

A dedicated drinking faucet at 0.5 gpm is fine for glasses and kettles. If the filter feeds your main faucet through a direct connection, slow flow becomes annoying quickly, and a high-flow design such as the Frizzlife SK99-NEW makes more sense. For RO, look at the output in gallons per day and whether there is a tank to buffer it.

A dedicated faucet needs a spare hole in the sink or counter, or a new one drilled, but it keeps full unfiltered flow at the main tap and makes each cartridge last longer because only drinking water passes through it. A direct-connect filter uses your existing faucet, which is simpler to install and wastes cartridge capacity on dishwashing water.

Check the replacement cartridge price and part number before you buy the system. Proprietary cartridges from established brands tend to stay available for years; generic listings sometimes disappear, leaving you with a housing that nothing fits.

sections.h: Installation: What You Need Under the Sink

blocks.p: Most under sink carbon filters are a one-hour job with basic tools, and none of them require soldering. The usual sequence is the same across brands: shut off the cold water angle stop, open the faucet to relieve pressure, fit the supplied tee adapter between the angle stop and the faucet supply line, mount the filter bracket to the cabinet wall, and run the push-fit tubing from the tee to the filter and from the filter to the faucet.

For a dedicated faucet, you need a hole. Many sinks have a spare knockout used for a sprayer or soap dispenser, and that is the easiest place to put it. If you need to drill a stone or quartz counter, that is a job for a diamond hole saw and a steady hand, or a countertop installer. Stainless sinks can be drilled with a step bit.

Reverse osmosis takes longer because it needs a drain connection. A drain saddle clamps onto the sink tailpiece above the trap, and the RO's waste line connects to it. Tank systems also need floor space in the cabinet for the tank, and tankless systems need an outlet. If your sink base has a garbage disposal, a dishwasher hose and a tangle of supply lines already, measure before you order. The G3P800's slim body is a large part of its appeal in a crowded cabinet.

After installation, flush the new cartridges as the manual directs, usually for several minutes, to clear carbon fines. Then check every push-fit joint for drips over the next day. A paper towel left under the fittings overnight is the simplest leak detector there is. If your sink drains slowly once everything is back in place, that is a separate problem; a [drain snake](/best-drain-snake/) is the quickest fix.

One rule applies to every filter on this page: connect it to the cold line only. Carbon filters are rated for cold water, and A.O. Smith's data sheet for the AO-US-200 states an operating range of 40 to 90°F. Hot water can damage cartridges and release what they have captured.

sections.h: The Real Cost Is the Cartridges

blocks.p: The starter kit price is a poor guide to what an under sink filter costs. Over five years, you will usually spend more on cartridges than on the system, so the honest comparison is the annual cartridge cost at your household's real usage.

Take the two certified carbon picks. The Claryum's cartridge set is rated for 600 gallons or six months, and the AO-US-200's for 500 gallons or six months. For most households the six-month limit arrives first, so both mean two cartridge sets a year. The Waterdrop 10UA's single cartridge is rated for up to 12 months, which halves the number of changes, but you are paying less for a narrower certification. That is a fair trade if taste is the goal and a false economy if lead is the goal.

Reverse osmosis has a staggered schedule. Waterdrop lists the G3P800's pre-filter at six months, its carbon block at 12 months and its membrane at 24 months. Tank systems like the RCC7AK use standard-size pre-filters that are inexpensive and widely available, with a membrane every couple of years and a remineralization cartridge on its own schedule. RO also has a hidden cost in water: whatever goes to the drain is water you pay for.

Two habits keep costs down. First, buy cartridges in a two-pack or annual bundle, which most makers discount. Second, set a reminder on your phone the day you install a cartridge, because most people overrun filter life by months, and a filter past its rated capacity is no longer doing the job it was certified for. Some systems include a faucet light or timer, but a calendar reminder works for all of them.

sections.h: When an Under Sink Filter Is the Wrong Answer

blocks.p: An under sink filter is the right tool for most kitchens, but not for every problem. Here is when to buy something else.

**You rent and cannot touch the plumbing.** Even a tool-free direct-connect install changes the supply line, and some leases prohibit it. A certified pitcher or a countertop unit is the renter's answer. Our [best water filter pitcher guide](/best-water-filter-pitcher/) ranks pitchers by the same certification rules used here, and several of them carry Standard 53 for lead.

**The problem is in every tap.** Rotten-egg smell from a well, iron staining in the toilet, sediment in the washing machine, or scale on every fixture are whole-house problems. Filtering one faucet does nothing for the rest. That calls for a point-of-entry system, which is covered in our [home water filtration guide](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/).

**The problem is in the shower.** If your complaint is dry skin, a chlorine smell when you shower, or hair that feels coated, an under sink filter will not help because it does not touch the bathroom. A shower filter is a small, cheap fix for that, with limits worth understanding; our [best shower head filter guide](/best-shower-head-filter/) explains what they can and cannot remove.

**The water may be microbiologically unsafe.** None of the carbon filters here are designed to make unsafe water safe to drink. If you are on a well that tests positive for bacteria, or under a boil-water notice, treat or boil the water as directed. Some RO systems include UV, as the G3P800 does, but a UV lamp is not a substitute for fixing a contaminated well.
**You do not know what is in your water.** Buying a filter before testing is the most common mistake in this category. Test, then buy the cheapest filter certified for what you found.

mistakes: Standard 372 certifies that the parts touching the water are made from lead-free materials. It says nothing about removing lead from your water. For lead reduction, look for NSF/ANSI 53 with lead named on the performance data sheet, as on the Claryum and AO-US-200, and ignore listing copy that blurs the two.
Buying reverse osmosis for city water that does not need it

RO costs more, wastes water down the drain, takes most of the cabinet and strips minerals. On municipal water with a clean report, a certified carbon filter handles chlorine, lead and PFAS. Reserve RO for wells and for reports that show high dissolved solids, nitrates, arsenic or fluoride.
Running cartridges past their rated capacity

Certified reductions only apply up to the rated gallons or months. A clogged or exhausted carbon block can stop reducing contaminants long before the flow drops noticeably. Set a calendar reminder when you install each cartridge and change it at whichever limit arrives first.
Connecting the filter to the hot line

Under sink carbon filters are designed for cold water only. Hot water can damage the cartridge and reduce its performance. Fit the tee to the cold angle stop, and use the hot tap for washing up, not for cooking water you want filtered.
Ignoring the cost of replacement cartridges

A cheap system with expensive or short-lived cartridges costs more over five years than a pricier system with long-lived ones. Check the replacement part number, price and rated life before you buy the starter kit, and buy from a brand whose cartridges will still be sold in five years.
bottomLine: Most kitchens should buy the Aquasana Claryum 3-Stage: certified to NSF/ANSI 42, 53 and 401, no tank, no drain line and no power. The A.O. Smith AO-US-200 gets you the same certifications for less if you accept shorter cartridge life, and the Waterdrop 10UA is the economical choice when taste is the only problem. Choose reverse osmosis only when your water report gives you a reason, then pick the iSpring RCC7AK for a proven tank system or the Waterdrop G3P800 to save cabinet space. Whatever you buy, check the certification against your water report first, and change the cartridges on time.

faqs.q: What is the best under sink water filter?
faqs.a: For most homes, the Aquasana Claryum 3-Stage. It is certified by the WQA to NSF/ANSI 42, 53 and 401, which covers chlorine taste, lead, PFOA/PFOS and many other contaminants, and it needs no tank, drain or power. If your water report shows high dissolved solids or nitrates, choose a reverse osmosis system instead.

faqs.q: Are under sink water filters worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you drink and cook with tap water. An under sink filter treats far more water than a pitcher at a lower cost per gallon, keeps filtered water on tap without refilling, and the certified models reduce health contaminants such as lead. They are not worth it if your water is already clean and you dislike the taste only slightly.

faqs.q: Does an under sink water filter remove lead?
faqs.a: Only if it is certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for lead. The Claryum 3-Stage and A.O. Smith AO-US-200 both carry that certification. Many cheaper filters advertise lead reduction while holding only NSF/ANSI 42 for taste and 372 for lead-free materials, which do not cover lead removal. Check the performance data sheet.

faqs.q: How often should I change an under sink water filter?
faqs.a: At the rated capacity or time limit, whichever comes first. That is six months for the Claryum and AO-US-200, up to 12 months for the Waterdrop 10UA, and staggered intervals of six to 24 months for RO stages. Heavy sediment or very high chlorine can shorten that, so change sooner if the flow drops.

faqs.q: Is reverse osmosis better than a carbon under sink filter?
faqs.a: It removes more, but it is not automatically better. RO reduces dissolved solids, nitrates, arsenic and fluoride that carbon cannot, but it wastes water, takes more space and strips minerals. On treated city water with a clean report, a certified carbon filter usually does everything needed at a lower running cost.

faqs.q: Can I install an under sink water filter myself?
faqs.a: Yes. Carbon filters typically take about an hour with an adjustable wrench and a drill for the bracket. You fit a tee to the cold supply, mount the filter and run push-fit tubing. A dedicated faucet needs a spare hole in the sink or counter. RO adds a drain saddle connection and, for tankless units, an outlet.

faqs.q: Does an under sink filter reduce water pressure?
faqs.a: At the filtered faucet, yes. Most certified carbon filters are rated around 0.5 gpm, and direct-connect units such as the Waterdrop 10UA at 0.75 gpm, which is slower than an unfiltered tap. High-flow designs like the Frizzlife SK99-NEW are rated up to 2.0 gpm. The rest of the house is not affected because only one line is filtered.
